title: EACC Secures Forfeiture of KSh426.8 Million Linked to Ex-Land Registrar
desc: EACC says the High Court has ordered forfeiture of KSh426.85 million in assets linked to former Kilifi Principal Land Registrar Felix Nyakundi and associates.
content:
The Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) has secured orders for the forfeiture of assets worth KSh426.85 million linked to former Kilifi Principal Land Registrar Felix Mecha Nyakundi, his wife Stellah Nyaboke Otwori and companies associated with the family.

EACC announced the development on Friday, September 25, following a judgment delivered by Justice Benjamin Musyoki at the Anti-Corruption and Economic Crimes Court on September 18, 2026.

The court found that the defendants had not satisfactorily explained the difference between the assets they acquired and their known legitimate sources of income.

The forfeiture covers money held in bank and mobile-money accounts, properties in Nairobi, Mombasa and Kilifi, three motor vehicles and KSh4.26 million in cash that had been recovered during a search operation.

According to EACC's case, investigations covered transactions and asset acquisitions between January 2013 and March 2024. During that period, investigators identified assets and transactions with a cumulative value of about KSh771.89 million.

The commission said the defendants were able to satisfactorily explain the acquisition of assets valued at KSh58.17 million, while the court ultimately ordered forfeiture of the assets it found to be unexplained and traceable.

Among the assets affected are properties linked to the family and their companies. Four Nairobi properties registered to The Bantu Hotel and Resort Company Limited are included in the forfeiture order, alongside properties in Mombasa and Kilifi.

The court also directed the relevant institutions to facilitate implementation of the orders. Banks and mobile-money service providers were directed to facilitate the transfer of applicable balances to the Government through EACC, while land authorities were directed to facilitate the transfer of the affected properties.

Importantly, the proceedings were asset-recovery proceedings rather than a criminal trial requiring EACC to prove a specific criminal offence. Citizen reported that the judgment found EACC was not required to establish a specific corrupt act to obtain forfeiture of unexplained assets under the applicable law.

The case therefore highlights the legal mechanism used by Kenyan authorities to recover assets that a respondent cannot satisfactorily demonstrate were acquired from legitimate sources.

For the public, the order means the identified assets will be transferred to the Government through the recovery process directed by the court, subject to implementation of the judgment.
